item.title: Symplectic Matroids, Stabilizer Codes, and Quantum Secret-Sharing
item.description:
Sayantan Ganguly

An $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear $[[n,k]]_q$ stabilizer code is represented by a totally isotropic subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^{2n}$ of dimension $n-k$, whose full-rank generator matrix has nonzero maximal minors on admissible column sets forming the bases of a representable symplectic matroid. Sarvepalli asked whether graphical symplectic matroids introduced by Chow give stabilizer codes with good parameters, when a Lagrangian matroid induces a quantum access structure, which code realizes it, and which polynomial carries the weight enumerator. We answer these questions. For a $3$-connected simple graph, every representation of a graphical symplectic matroid, over any field, gives a stabilizer code of distance exactly $2$, so the girth is not a lower bound. For a represented Lagrangian matroid and a dealer, we construct the dealer-shortened stabilizer code, its logical operators, an encoding isometry and explicit recovery maps, and we show that this is the code implemented by the stabilizer state through teleportation. A set of players recovers the secret, learns nothing, or learns part of it according to a rank formula on pairs of columns, which equals its mutual information with the dealer; for graph states it becomes a cut-rank condition. Over $\F_2$ a symplectic matroid of any rank has only one representation, so the code, its access structure and its weight enumerators depend on the matroid alone; for $q\ge3$ even the enumerator does not. Circuit-induced authorized sets always reconstruct when the matroid is self-dual, but not in general, and a six-qubit graph state shows that the two access structures can differ even then. Finally, a polynomial in the ranks of column pairs determines both weight enumerators.

item.title: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding
item.description:
Cory T. Aitchison, Lucas H. English, Benjamin Béri, Dominic J. Williamson, Campbell K. McLauchlan

Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance. However, theoretical studies of quantum error correction typically assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. Here we model decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels by treating physical error rates as random variables. We show that the decoding performance is set by a small number of information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: the entropy determines the threshold while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Furthermore, our results give a quantitative measure of the benefits of characterizing this noise. We numerically investigate both maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes, showing good agreement with theory across the code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise settings, including with noise distributions seen in open-access superconducting devices. When it comes to error correction in realistic settings, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions could therefore be more informative than the mean or median error rates of a device's components.

item.title: Optimal Error corrected Hamiltonian estimation with nuisance parameters
item.description:
Zhiyao Hu, Haidong Yuan, Liang Jiang, Zain H. Saleem

Realistic quantum sensing is often affected by both noise and unknown nuisance parameters. Under Markovian dynamics, existing error correction approaches have often sought to suppress nuisance responses alongside environmental noise. Here we show that this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and can be overly restrictive: nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose fundamentally different constraints and require distinct treatments. We establish a general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time dependent Hamiltonian, in the presence of both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that attain it. Our results show that to achieve Heisenberg scaling Markovian noise must be suppressed locally by quantum error correction, whereas nuisance parameters need not, and in general should not, be eliminated locally. Instead, optimally designed coherent control can separate their accumulated effects from the target signal over the full sensing evolution. Consequently, Heisenberg scaling can remain attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise. This distinction substantially enlarges the regime in which Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general principle for designing robust quantum sensors.

item.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
item.description:
Chenyang Jin, Susanne F. Yelin, Andi Gu

Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
item.description:
Stefano Tinelli, Francisco Lázaro, Francisco García Herrero

A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

item.title: Quantifying the irrealism required by quantum random access codes
item.description:
Pedro R. Dieguez

How far must decoding observables be from having elements of reality to achieve a given quantum advantage in a communication task? We answer this question for quantum random access codes. Here, an observable has an element of reality when its unrevealed measurement leaves the preparation undisturbed; its irrealism is the relative entropy to the closest such preparation. Because it comprises local coherence and the correlations destroyed by the unrevealed measurement, irrealism applies to prepare-and-measure (PM) and entanglement-assisted (EA) codes alike. For PM codes decoded in mutually unbiased bases, we obtain the irrealism frontier, the least total irrealism compatible with each success probability, exactly in every dimension; an excess-irrealism identity shows that Gibbs states of the decoding operator attain it uniquely. For PM codes minimized also over the decoders, the required irrealism vanishes up to the classical value and is positive beyond it; for qubits, mutually unbiased decoders are not the cheapest below a success probability of 0.833. For EA codes with a qubit receiver, trusted decoders, and parity-dependent sender settings, the frontier exceeds the PM one by the realism-based nonlocality of the contexts used by an optimal code, and with rank-one projective sender measurements a success probability above 0.815 certifies a minimum realism-based nonlocality of the shared state.

item.title: Stitching Quantum Codes into Quilts: Universal Logic with no Ancillary Qubits
item.description:
Stasiu Wolanski

Proposals abound for performing fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between quantum codes beyond the surface code. We introduce a new construction, the code quilt, whereby a target joint logical operator of two or more codeblocks is directly measured without the use of an ancillary system. We construct explicit circuits to perform a logical measurement using the quilt construction, which also require no physical qubits beyond the ancillas already in place to perform idle syndrome extraction on the codeblocks in question. We give a detailed structural analysis of the construction, which is based on a subsystem code, and provide several sets of sufficient conditions under which the relevant code-capacity distance is preserved. We give two variants of the protocol. The first, where the gauge generators of the subsystem code are measured directly, is provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but admits a particularly practical circuit implementation in which the physical qubit degree increases by at most two. The second has more favourable asymptotic properties, although we do not prove its fault tolerance in the general case. We then perform an extensive empirical analysis of the technique, in particular of the first variant, as applied to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, finding code-capacity-distance preserving quilts for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators. We optimise to find sparse and decongested detector bases for each and, for a randomly selected subset, find circuits that we estimate to be distance preserving. Finally, we perform decoding experiments on a subset of these circuits and find that their logical error probability is comparable to that of idle memory for operations involving the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between $1.5\times 10^{-3}$ and $3\times 10^{-3}$.

item.title: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction
item.description:
Eduardo Dueñez, Edgar Said Hernandez Sanchez, Edgar A. Duéñez-Guzmán, Suzanne Sadedin

Quantum computation entails robustness engineering: a noisy quantum state is measured continuously, and a classical algorithm (the decoder) must infer corrections that reliably remove the noise, fast enough to keep up. We write several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), and search over it with grammatical evolution. Written in the language, the published decoders show their parameters in plain view, allowing us to re-parameterise BP+OSD (ordered statistics decoding) and BP+LSD (localized statistics decoding) decoders with damping, before any search, making each 17.1--41.0$\times$ faster at a higher error rate, and BP+OSD-0 about 103 faster than the ldpc package's version tuned on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution over the language finds decoders that improve the time-error front. One makes 23% fewer logical errors than BP+OSD-0 with damping at 0.64$\times$ its time, and decoders evolved from random code are more accurate than ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less. Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.

item.title: Structure-Guided Synthesis of Low-Error Syndrome Extraction Circuits
item.description:
Shanchuan Li, Xin Hong, Pengcheng Zhu, Xiangzhen Zhou, Fanxu Meng, Shenggang Ying

Gate orders can change fault propagation and logical error rates even when syndrome-extraction circuits implement the same ideal stabilizer measurements. Optimizing these orderings independently for every check, however, becomes computationally demanding as code size increases. We present a synthesis method for structured Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes that groups checks by recurring connectivity and shares one relative gate order per group, reducing independent ordering choices. A CP-SAT solver jointly determines the shared orders and the execution time of each physical gate, enforcing resource and measurement constraints across the circuit. Noisy circuit simulations with decoding then guide the selection of the final circuit. We compare with state-of-the-art approaches, including Auto-Stabilizer-Check (ASC), PropHunt, and AlphaSyndrome. Across 15 quantum low-density parity-check codes from ten code families, our method achieves the lowest logical error rate estimates. Relative to ASC, the strongest baseline in our evaluation, the median reduction is 11.4% and the largest is 38.6%. Our circuits improve circuit-level distance over ASC on ten instances and preserve the code distance in seven. Across five timed codes, our method reduces the mean time to the first feasible circuit by factors of 21.4-136.6 relative to ASC, at equal or lower depth.

item.title: Parallel transversal entangling gates for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing
item.description:
Katrin Bolsmann, Alan Kahan, Alejandro Bermúdez, Markus Müller

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity entangling gates that can be implemented efficiently across multiple qubit pairs. We present a scheme for simultaneous pairwise entangling operations, i.e., a transversal controlled-$Z$ gate, across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion architecture. A tailored dynamical decoupling scheme suppresses unwanted couplings with a pulse count that scales quadratically with the number of ions. We show that incorporating a genuine geometric cancellation reduces the pulse count and, for selected register sizes, allows the parallel operation to be completed faster than an equivalent sequence of two-qubit gates while requiring a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency. We assess the experimental feasibility of the protocol by analyzing the impact of decoherence and crosstalk arising from laser wave-vector misalignment. To gain insight into the robustness of fault-tolerant protocols against realistic imperfections of the proposed transversal gate scheme, we investigate how crosstalk-induced gate errors affect the fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state between two $[[4,1,2]]$ quantum-error-detection code blocks. These results highlight the potential of transversal entangling gates as a building block for trapped-ion-based scalable fault-tolerant quantum error correction.

item.title: Syndrome-based Calibration Using Gate-Error Amplification
item.description:
Andrew T. Kamen, Arielle Sanford, Frederic T. Chong, Andy J. Goldschmidt, Siddharth Dangwal

We present Gate-Error Amplification for Recalibration with Syndromes (GEARS), a runtime calibration framework that uses gate-error amplification to efficiently tune control parameters during quantum error correction. Maintaining reliable control of large qubit arrays throughout hours-long computations requires repeated calibration to compensate for hardware drift. In conventional calibration, targeted qubits are temporarily removed from the code, introducing non-negligible space-time overhead. An elegant alternative uses syndrome information already collected during error correction as feedback for in situ recalibration, but acquiring signal requires sufficient (1) measurement budget or (2) probe strength, i.e., the size of deliberate control perturbations. More measurements improve statistical precision but result in slower control updates, while stronger perturbations produce larger calibration signals at the cost of additional errors. GEARS augments syndrome-based calibration with an established gate characterization technique called gate-error amplification. Our approach repeats selected CZ gates and probes their controls in spatially separated groups, strengthening local calibration signals while limiting the logical cost of probing. Surface code simulations show that GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements by approximately a factor of eight at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength. In closed-loop calibration, GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces excess expected logical failures by approximately 31-40% relative to calibration without amplification across the evaluated execution windows. Under time-dependent drift, GEARS increases the estimated critical drift frequency by approximately 1.9x. These results indicate that deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation can improve the long-time performance of quantum computations.

item.title: Counterfactual attribution of surface-code failures under non-Pauli noise: dependence on trajectory pairing
item.description:
Kisung Jin, Gyuil Cha

Under Pauli noise in a stabilizer memory, attributing a quantum error-correction failure to the noise that caused it has a canonical answer; under non-Pauli noise the attribution depends on how trajectories are paired with their counterfactuals. We define a failing shot's cause set, the sites whose removal alone removes the failure, and separate it from pairing-independent net effects. The pairing enters wherever a fixed random draw meets a Born probability; making it maximal at every random step selects shared random numbers, while continuity does not. In a distance-three surface code, exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl fail at rates equivalent within a registered margin, yet under shared draws 20.2% of exact-noise failures need three or more sites, against 2.3% under the twirl. Other admissible pairings move the mean coherent cause count from 1.61 to 80 times the minimum the marginals allow, yet pairing-independent quantities barely separate the two models. Shot-level attributions should therefore state their pairing and report pairing-independent effects alongside.

item.title: Compiling Constraints into Neuromorphic Ising Machines
item.description:
Faiek Ahsan, Shantanu Chakrabartty

Most practical combinatorial optimization problems involve constraints, and an Ising machine that flips one spin at a time can respect them only through energy penalties that raise barriers between feasible solutions. Here we show that a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine can enforce constraints through programmable transitions rather than penalties. In an autoencoder-like architecture, each inner-layer neuron represents a move, a family of multi-spin transitions that maps every feasible state to another feasible state, receives the energy change of its move through connections that outer-layer neurons multiplicatively switch on or off, and updates the state through the same connections. A compiler turns constraints into this wiring with a number of auxiliary clauses that grows only polynomially for parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition and permutation constraints. Restricting the search to feasible states reduces constraint handling to move design, and we show that the fastest-annealing moves are not those that mix fastest but those that lower the deepest energy barriers, and that moves chosen from the objective lower them further than random ones. On third-order graph matching, the machine needs orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines. Configured as a sampler on a field-programmable gate array, it decodes the surface code with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to code distance 15 within 52 $μ$s per shot and, under noisy syndrome measurements, decodes in real time for millisecond measurement rounds up to distance 9 with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders.

item.title: Certified Separation Between Coherent and Adaptive Temporal Processing of Quantum-Error-Correction Readout
item.description:
Shreya Savadatti, Matthew Reynolds, Jonathan Maack, Wesley Jones, Franz Franchetti

Repeated quantum-error-correction readout is normally converted into a classical time series: each syndrome pulse is measured on arrival and only the resulting classical record is retained. Nonorthogonal readout signals raise the question of whether preserving quantum information between rounds can improve the final recovery decision. We formulate this comparison as a loss-weighted state-discrimination problem. For an idealized two-round benchmark with quadrature phase-shift-keying (QPSK) signals, a receiver with a seven-dimensional persistent register has certified recovery-decision error below $24.2100\%$, whereas every separate adaptive receiver has error above $25.1431\%$. The certified separation is at least $0.933$ percentage points. The loss counts incorrect final error-mask decisions in the benchmark. In the strict architecture, where the counted register is the entire persistent state, four dimensions are necessary and sufficient to outperform the adaptive class. Certified separations also occur at three and four rounds with register dimensions $8$ and $36$, compared with $16$ and $64$ for full-prefix storage. We relate memory dimension to the structure of the temporal measurement, give a sufficient memory bound for collective measurements, and quantify robustness to register dephasing and accumulated channel error.

item.title: Generalizing and Combining Check Constructions: Design-Space Exploration for Fault-Tolerant Quantum State Preparation
item.description:
Ludwig Schmid, Robert Wille

Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs logical states prepared such that single faults cannot spread into uncorrectable errors. Post-selection achieves this with added checks that detect dangerous faults and discard the run. How the checks are measured sets the depth and operation count of the circuit, and the best trade-off depends on the hardware. Existing automated methods, however, each use one check construction and yield fixed trade-offs. We first introduce Block Checks, in which several checks share one fault-tolerantly prepared auxiliary block, which places them and existing constructions in a single design space. Second, to explore that space, we propose a Pareto tree search that adds checks and auxiliary blocks, merges auxiliaries, and edits the circuit. On quantum codes of distance up to seven, the search finds best-known circuits for many new operation--depth trade-offs and surpasses existing methods. The code is open source as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT) at https://github.com/munich-quantum-toolkit/qecc, and all circuits are available in the QECirc library at https://qecirc.com.

item.title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities
item.description:
Q. Rumman Rahman, S. M. Girvin, D. K. Weiss

The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: The Clifford Hierarchy from Clifford Stabilizers in 2D
item.description:
Alison Warman, Sakura Schafer-Nameki

The Bravyi-König theorem limits the constant-depth logical gates of 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes to be in the Clifford group. Known qubit codes with Clifford stabilizers exceed it by only one level of the Clifford hierarchy, and this was conjectured to hold generally. We show that this bound can be completely bypassed, and that topological codes with Clifford stabilizers in 2D can realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy. We present two explicit constructions of codes based on copies of the quantum doubles of $D_4$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2$, with $k$ logical qubits and a logical $C^{k-1}Z$ gate, which is at level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy. The physical circuits realizing the gates consist only of physical $Z$ or $CZ$ gates. The main new ingredient comes from the logical encoding, which depends crucially on non-Abelian group multiplication.

item.title: The limits of magic-state cultivation
item.description:
Llorenç Balada Gaggioli, Jakub Mareček

Fault tolerance is understood through Pauli algebra, which fails at non-Clifford gates. Circuits such as magic-state cultivation, which checks an encoded T state with physical T gates, have therefore lacked an exact theory of which faults are harmful. We develop such a theory and show that, for any circuit that prepares a magic state with non-Clifford gates and postselection, one stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates decides which faults are harmful. This ties cultivation to distillation, bounds its T-count from below and gives an exact test. For a single check on an ideally encoded state, the fault distance reduces to Pauli algebra on the code. As a use case, we analyze the S gates that have stood in for T gates in the design of cultivation. We show that this proxy can only overstate the fault distance of such a check, and that the checks in use, on color and surface codes, tolerate at most half as many faults as their code allows. The theory also yields nearest-neighbor checks that keep the full distance, certified up to code distance nine.

item.title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
item.description:
Christopher Kang, Alexander Cowtan, Adam Bene Watts, Guillaume Dauphinais, Benjamin Ide

Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program. In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection. We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous $Z$- and $X$-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.

item.title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
item.description:
Aleksandra Świerkowska, Ilgaz Er, Emmanouil Giortamis, Pramod Bhatotia

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict $1\,μ\text{s}$ cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within $1\,μ\text{s}$ while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the $1\,μ\text{s}$ deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in $144\,\text{ns}$, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.

item.title: Stabilizer models of achiral abelian topological orders
item.description:
Marvin Qi, Wilbur Shirley

We construct continuous-variable stabilizer codes realizing every achiral 2D abelian topological order, both bosonic and fermionic. Starting from an arbitrary signature-zero integer $K$-matrix, we show that the corresponding topological order can be obtained by condensing a lattice of dyons with trivial pairwise mutual braiding in an $\mathbb{R}^N$ gauge theory. We implement this condensation microscopically by gauging a non-on-site 1-form symmetry of the $\mathbb{R}^N$ toric code.

item.title: Reliability of quantum communication over erasure channels
item.description:
Hongyu Mao, Kun Fang

Quantum information can be reliably transmitted at rates below the quantum capacity with an error that vanishes as the number of channel uses grows. The reliability function characterizes the optimal exponential decay rate of this error. For quantum erasure channels with a prime input dimension, we determine the reliability function exactly at all positive communication rates below capacity that meet or exceed an explicit critical rate. Notably, stabilizer coding strategies attain this optimal reliability throughout this regime.

item.title: Accelerating Quantum Error Correction Simulations under Coherent Noise with Compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States
item.description:
Jiale Huang, Yaojian Chen, Ke Liu, Dingshun Lv, Mingpu Qin

Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance $d=9$ and on the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.

item.title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
item.description:
Louis Follet, Paavai Pari, Isidor Schoch, Thien Nguyen, Justin G. Lietz, Daniel Lowell, und 4 weitere

Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.

item.title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
item.description:
Christopher A. Pattison, Jeongwan Haah, John Preskill

Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with $n$ physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$ logical qubits, where $ε$ is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to ${\sf polylog}(n/ε)$.

item.title: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols
item.description:
Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Guanyu Zhu

Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, we construct quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with distances $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$ and at least $N^{1-ε}$ individually addressable logical CCZ gates on pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits, for every fixed $0<ε<1$. With all logical qubits outside these triples initialized to $|0\rangle$, any subset of the corresponding logical CCZ gates can be implemented with a transversal physical CCZ circuit. As applications, we obtain two nearly optimal magic state protocols: CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent $γ\rightarrow 0$ and error suppression of nearly linear order, and a magic state fountain that directly prepares $N^{1-ε}$ encoded CCZ magic states with nearly linear distance $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$. The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers. The assumption concerns Reed--Solomon codes on three subfields of characteristic two and pairwise coprime extension degrees, a local hypothesis studied in a companion manuscript. We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.

item.title: Parity Push Post-Selection with Soft Parity Constraints for Quantum LDPC Codes
item.description:
Hong Jun Kim, Gun Sik Min, Seok-Hyung Lee, Jun Heo

Post-selection lowers the logical error rate of a quantum error-correcting code by rejecting unreliable shots. For a code with $K$ logical observables, the logical gap, a standard post-selection criterion, involves $2^K$ logical classes, and existing approximations to it suffer from a non-convergence error floor or a shielding effect. We introduce a decoder-agnostic post-selection strategy for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, called parity push post-selection (PPPS), which re-decodes a shot once per logical observable with a push toward the opposite parity. Each push adds one check node and one variable node to the Tanner graph of the detector error model, and we accept a shot only when every re-decoding returns a solution in the original logical class. We show that, with degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding, PPPS accepts a shot exactly when the logical gap exceeds the push strength $λ$. Applied with the Relay-BP decoder to the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code at $p=10^{-3}$ and the [[144,12,12]] code at $p=3\times10^{-3}$ under circuit-level depolarizing noise, PPPS lowers the logical error rate by factors of about 50 and 75, respectively, at rejection rates near 1%. We observe that PPPS rejects failures that prior post-selection strategies cannot reject, and thus shows improved performance.

item.title: Singlet flags: using native entanglement to restore the circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon
item.description:
William Chow, Jonathan Baugh

High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could greatly reduce the qubit count of silicon spin-qubit processors, but their checks are long-range and of high weight. Shuttling one ancilla electron through every data qubit of a check measures such checks, but a single fault on the ancilla spreads to several data qubits, so the circuit distance can fall far below the code distance. We make the mobile ancilla one half of a spin singlet whose partner stays at home; a Bell measurement at the end of the check provides a flag for isolated bit-flip faults acquired during the walk. Using new distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10 and 12, and exact circuit distances from two independent solvers, we show that without the flag the circuit distance falls as check weight grows, to 1 at weight 12, while with it every weight-8 and weight-10 code recovers circuit distance 5 or 6 and corrects as many faults as the code. For codes of distance 8 to 12 the flag raises the circuit distance by one to four, and the Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. In circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits, the flag lowers logical error rates by typically 2-10x across bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation and surface codes, and the gain survives percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet's electrons. BP+OSD does not reach the full circuit distance of the flagged circuits, so our flagged logical error rates are upper bounds: decoding the same shots exactly raises the flag's gain on the distance-6 codes from 3-7x to 5-17x for the weight-6 BB code, and from 1-12x to 5-90x at weights 8 and 10 for p >= 2.5x10^-4.

item.title: High-rate low-distance color codes
item.description:
Peter-Jan H. S. Derks, Lucas Berent, Mark Webster, Robert Wille, Jens Eisert, Aleksander Kubica

Experimental implementations of two-dimensional color codes encoding a single logical qubit have surpassed the fidelity of physical qubits. A natural next step is to investigate higher-rate codes that encode multiple logical qubits. Here we propose small, high-rate 2D color codes for this purpose. We design distance-$3$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/3$ and distance-$4$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/4$. We prove that these rates are optimal for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with non-negative Euler characteristic. We benchmark the codes by simulating Steane-style error correction with real-time feedback and no post-selection in a linear trapped-ion chain model with all-to-all connectivity. The two best-performing codes have parameters $[[20,4,4]]$ and $[[16,4,4]]$ and achieve break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of $0.22\%$ and $0.26\%$, respectively. These results match the performance of Shor-style error correction with bivariate bicycle codes that use weight-$5$ measurements.

item.title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
item.description:
Hansol Noh, Unam Oh, Sangkyu Baek, Doyeol, Ahn

Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

item.title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
item.description:
Luca Hofele, Yongxin Song, Áron Márton, Ian Hesner, Ilya Besedin, Jakob Ekert, und 13 weitere

Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
item.description:
Evan McKinney, Kun Liu, Harshvardhan K. Babla, Robert J. Schoelkopf, Yongshan Ding

Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical $\mathrm{CR}_z$ has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8\% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1\% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3\% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.

item.title: Quantum Codes for Distributed Quantum Fault Sensing
item.description:
Xiu-Hao Deng

Targeted recovery in modular quantum processors requires identifying the component affected by a fault. Independent qubits can monitor faults through repeated preparation and measurement. Bell-pair probes improve the guaranteed correct-site probability for unknown local channels, but require partners kept away from the fault. Can entanglement among exposed probes supply this advantage without protected storage? We establish a quantum-code criterion for optimal distributed fault sensing of one unknown local qubit channel with strength in a prescribed positive range. For one interrogation with zero false alarms and no background noise, suitable code states attain the optimal worst-case correct-site probability, improving on independent probes by 50% with every qubit exposed. Exact attainment is equivalent to mutually orthogonal input and single-qubit Pauli error subspaces. Pairwise entanglement gives no improvement, and entanglement depth at most four cannot exceed 95.54% of the optimum without protected ancillas. Approaching the optimum without protected ancillas also requires a number of probes proportional to the array size to participate in larger entangled factors. For a persistent fault under memoryless depolarizing background of fixed strength 0 < eta < 1, independent probes already attain the optimal logarithmic interrogation scaling at fixed success between zero and one and a positive false-alarm budget. In three 1000-site comparisons with specified readouts, an encoded-probe protocol certifies fewer interrogations than independent probes and only one more than optimally decoded ideal Bell pairs, while storing no protected qubits.

item.title: Optimal Measurement Rounds for Perfect Encoded Fusion
item.description:
Seita Tsuboi, Takuya Kasamura, Leo Itoh, Motoharu Tsuboi, Tomohiro Hatori, Junichiro Kadomoto

Encoded fusion combines probabilistic physical fusions to perform a logical Bell measurement. Adaptive choices depend on earlier measurement outcomes and therefore require multiple measurement rounds. We determine the minimum worst-case number of rounds for perfect fusion of two blocks of an irreducible [[n,1]] stabilizer code. A strategy is perfect if the logical Bell measurement succeeds on every branch containing at least one successful physical fusion. Even after fixing the past history, including measurement values, we consider all success/failure branches, including those with zero probability for a particular input state or measurement device. In a lossless model with fixed coordinate pairing, arbitrary Pauli failure bases, and each pair fused exactly once, the optimum equals the minimum root eccentricity over the local complementation orbit of rooted graphs representing the code. The lower bound applies to arbitrary perfect strategies that choose batches and bases using previous outcomes. We also characterize the batch sequences that can occur on an all-failure branch of a perfect strategy by a necessary and sufficient graph adjacency condition. A matching strategy fuses distance layers from the outside in and, after the first success, completes the remaining fusions in at most one further round by changing the failure bases along an induced path.

item.title: Logical error prediction and geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased circuit-level noise
item.description:
Youshin Chung, Yujin Kang, Jun Heo

Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. Geometries selected by the model are validated through direct biased circuit-level simulations. At a physical error rate of 0.004 and a target logical error rate of 10^{-3}, the validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models, respectively, relative to unrotated square codes. These results provide a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design.

item.title: CHEQ: A Concurrent Hardware Evaluation Platform for QEC Decoders via Batch-Invariant Circuit-Level Noise Sampling
item.description:
Sechan Park, Kyeongwon Lee, Mundo Jung, Chaebin Jung, Woojoo Lee

Hardware quantum error correction (QEC) decoders require validation of logical error suppression and timing compliance before deployment. Rare logical failures and deadline violations demand extensive sampling, while algorithm-level software evaluation does not directly measure hardware response times. Circuit-level noise models contain many error mechanisms but few firings per shot at low physical error rates, making exhaustive per-shot scanning inefficient. We present CHEQ, an FPGA platform integrating on-chip sampling, concurrent decoder evaluation, scoring, and RISC-V control. Its Sampling Units use geometric skipping to sample firing locations from detector error models and amortize mechanism traversal across shots within each batch. Under independent random draws and exact geometric sampling, the shot distribution is invariant to batch size, enabling a memory-throughput tradeoff. A throughput model guides joint selection of the Sampling Unit count, batch size, and decoder count under FPGA resource constraints. Across evaluated conditions, the pooled one-sided 95% upper bound on the weighted root-mean-square relative firing-rate difference from Stim is 0.16%. At a batch size of 4,096, a Sampling Unit uses only 4.8%-11.2% of a Helios decoder's LUTs for code distances 7, 9, 11, and 13. On an AMD VCU118 FPGA at code distance 7 and physical error rate 10^-3, two Sampling Units supply 20 Helios decoders at 49.2 million shots/s, completing 10^10 shots in 3.4 minutes without host-side shot generation.

item.title: MASQ: Measurement-Adaptive Sampling for Near-Clifford Quantum Error Correction Circuits
item.description:
Chaebin Jung, Sangmin Jeon, Kyeongwon Lee, Sechan Park, Woojoo Lee

Classical sampling of quantum error correction (QEC) circuits supports fault-tolerant protocol evaluation, but estimating rare logical failures requires many independent shots. Frame-active-state simulators isolate non-stabilizer information in a dense active-state vector, yet dense-state processing remains exponential in the active width. This paper presents MASQ, an exact measurement-adaptive sampler for near-Clifford QEC circuits based on selective materialization of non-Clifford rotations. At each measurement boundary, MASQ materializes only rotations in a measurement-relevant closure capturing direct and indirect non-commuting dependencies, deferring the rest to limit active-state expansion. Stabilizer-assisted elimination further removes rotations certified to be invisible to all future measurements. A circuit-dependent schedule is computed once and shared across shots, while adaptive caching of conditional Born probabilities and batched execution reduce repeated sampling work while preserving the measurement-record distribution. Across 19 QEC benchmarks, MASQ reduces peak active width by up to 40 active virtual qubits and achieves up to 8,098-fold CPU throughput speedup over Clifft on multi-round circuits.

item.title: Magic state cultivation with lattice-surgery escape on superconducting hardware
item.description:
Haoran Liao, Michael Schutzman, William Munizzi, Pranav Mundada, Gavin Hartnett, Yuval Baum

Magic state cultivation (MSC) is a low-overhead protocol for fault-tolerantly preparing logical magic states. In this work, we implement two MSC variants to prepare a magic state in a distance-5 code on a publicly available IBM Nighthawk processor. The first is a lattice-surgery escape, recently proposed by Hirano et al. and experimentally studied here for the first time. The second is a grafting escape, previously demonstrated by Rosenfeld et al., and extended here by incorporating a switch into a matchable code. Both protocols begin with fault-tolerant cultivation of a T state on a color code, followed by an escape into a larger code. We decode the results using minimum-weight perfect matching or Tesseract on circuit-level error models calibrated to the hardware noise. Compared with the previous experiment, our cultivated T state achieves a logical error probability of 2e-5 at the T-state injection angle, nearly 10x lower with about 3x the retainment. Moreover, our execution of the grafting escape has a 2x lower logical error rate per stabilizer round at a higher retainment. When comparing the two protocols under identical execution conditions and complementary gap postselection based on decoder confidence, lattice-surgery escape into the surface code preserves a T-state fidelity above 0.99 ten rounds after escape at about 5% retainment. By contrast, matchable-switched grafting drops below 0.95 fidelity at comparable retainment. Furthermore, the lattice-surgery escape reaches a logical error rate per stabilizer round of about 0.14% with around 11% average shot retainment. These results establish lattice-surgery escape as a practical MSC protocol that benefits from a direct transition into a surface code, and demonstrate the lowest MSC error and the highest surface-code magic-state fidelity reported to date, advancing the experimental realization of fault-tolerant non-Clifford gadgets.

item.title: Simplifying models of noisy stabilizer QEC on leakage qubits by Pauli twirling
item.description:
Alex Kwiatkowski, Aaron J. Friedman

The growing capabilities of quantum error-correction (QEC) experiments make it increasingly important to develop methods that predict or assess logical performance over many QEC cycles. Prior work has shown that a stabilizer QEC cycle subject to Pauli-stochastic noise can be modeled by a classical Markov process over syndrome states, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each syndrome transition. Here, we extend this framework to systems in which physical qubits are subject to leakage. We first develop the theory of leakage-dephased Pauli twirling and show that twirled processes can be expressed in terms of Pauli maps on the computational subspace, conditioned on transitions between leakage patterns. We apply this theory to noisy stabilizer QEC with leakage, demonstrating that a QEC cycle with leakage can be modeled by a classical Markov process over the joint syndrome and leakage patterns, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each joint transition. Finally, we derive a transfer-matrix description of repeated QEC cycles and an exact transfer-matrix expression for the success probability of a QEC memory experiment. This framework connects leaky error models of the individual components of the QEC cycle to many-cycle logical performance and provides a foundation for logical characterization and benchmarking methods that can account for leakage.

item.title: Probing the real-time decoding accuracy bounds in trapped ion architectures
item.description:
Arianna Meinking, Evangelia Takou, Kenneth R. Brown

Fault tolerant quantum computers will rely on real-time decoders that process syndromes faster than the QEC cycle duration. The millisecond cycle times offered by trapped ion platforms relax low-latency decoding demands, but simulations and experiments have not yet exploited this time budget to reach maximum logical error suppression. We show how a hybrid sliding window decoding scheme composed of a lower-accuracy and a higher-accuracy decoder can yield substantially improved logical error rates, while preserving low latency. All windows are handled by the lower-accuracy decoder, with some windows being infrequently switched to the higher-accuracy decoder. We extract soft-output information from the lower-accuracy decoder efficiently for any QLDPC code, which allows us to identify decoding windows of low confidence. We simulate memory experiments of bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, using trapped-ion informed noise models. Depending on the physical error rate and BB code, we find up to 3-4 orders of magnitude logical error rate reduction compared to the $\texttt{BP-LSD}$ decoder, and up to 2-3 orders of magnitude lower logical error rate compared to the $\texttt{Beamsearch}$ decoder. By leveraging available classical processing time, our decoding protocol significantly boosts decoding accuracy, ultimately reducing the demands on increasing code size.

item.title: Black holes as black boxes: a query lower bound on python's lunch decoding
item.description:
Chris Waddell, Michelle Xu

The python's lunch conjecture relates the complexity of bulk reconstruction in holographic tensor networks to an exponential cost associated with post-selection. We establish a tight query lower bound for this decoding problem in a Haar random oracle model, with a python's lunch circuit that applies Haar random unitary $U$ to a logical input and fixed ancillas, followed by post-selection on $m$ output qubits. Given one copy of the normalized encoded state and coherent oracle access to $U$ and $U^\dagger$, including controlled queries, we prove that recovering even a single logical bit with constant average advantage requires $Ω(2^{m/2})$ queries. Together with the state-independent amplitude amplification upper bound for approximately isometric encodings, this establishes query complexity $Θ(2^{m/2})$ at constant decoding accuracy. We also comment on the decoding cost for other "admissible'" ensembles of unitaries $U$ which give rise to families of approximately isometric holographic maps.

item.title: QEDist: Practical Exact Distance Certification for Stabilizer Codes
item.description:
Jong Yeon Lee

We present QEDist, a method and software package that certifies the distance of qubit stabilizer codes. Building on tree-search methods, QEDist constructs candidate logical operators one qubit at a time, using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, and verified symmetries to reduce the work. For a cutoff $W$, a completed search either finds a nontrivial logical operator of weight at most $W$ or proves that none exists. Because satisfying one check can violate another, we use both satisfied and unsatisfied checks to lower-bound the weight needed to complete a logical operator, and prune branches whose bound exceeds the remaining budget, which substantially reduces net search time. We benchmark QEDist mainly on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes; the same formulation extends to non-CSS codes and to the fault distance of syndrome-extraction circuits. For lifted-product (LP) codes, we further exploit the product structure to replace part of the full-code search with a smaller search on a classical constituent. We establish exact distances for codes with up to several thousand qubits, including Abelian and non-Abelian LP codes whose distances were previously reported only as upper bounds. In several seconds of search on one laptop core, QEDist certifies exact distances up to 20 for many of these codes and fault distance 10 for the syndrome-extraction circuit of the $[[144,12,12]]$ code. With orders-of-magnitude speedups over the tested exact solvers, QEDist makes exact distance certification a practical tool for selecting and optimizing finite-length quantum codes.

item.title: Resolving and Suppressing Temporally Correlated Noise in Quantum Error Correction
item.description:
Alec Eickbusch, Nick Noll, Michael Newman, Matt McEwen, Leigh S. Martin, Alexis Morvan, und 356 weitere

Scaling fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) requires suppressing errors in both space and time, yet standard logical memory experiments primarily probe spatial faults. Here, we use a 105-qubit Willow superconducting quantum processor to realize and scale the surface code stability experiment, which is alternatively sensitive to temporal error chains. Scaling from patch sizes of $3 \times 3$ to $7 \times 7$, we realize a timelike block suppression factor of $μ_T = 1.47 \pm 0.25$, demonstrating the ability to maintain temporal error suppression as the number of qubits increases. By extending the stability experiment for many cycles, we uncover a sum-of-exponentials behavior in error suppression caused by a temporally correlated error: data-qubit heating to the third excited state $|3\rangle$. We fully capture this effect with a parameter-free, device-level leakage model incorporating higher-state transport during syndrome extraction cycles. To suppress this error, we develop and realize a walking stability circuit, reaching a logical error probability floor of $\le 3.20\times 10^{-8}$ at 60 cycles---two orders of magnitude below the standard construction---and limited by ionizing radiation error bursts. Finally, by adaptively terminating syndrome extraction based on decoder confidence in an offline analysis, we reduce spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% compared to the optimal fixed-cycle strategy.

item.title: The speed limit of gravitational entanglement and the cost of noise
item.description:
Ekta Panwar, Anubhav Chaturvedi

Is gravity quantum? A proposed test lets two small masses, each in a superposition of two places, become entangled through their mutual gravity. Gravity is weak, so the masses must stay coherent for seconds while random forces disturb them. Here we ask how fast gravity can entangle two masses, and what noise costs. Without noise we find the maximum rate exactly: it falls as the inverse cube of the separation, and two positions per mass achieve it. Above a noise level set by the masses and their separation, gravity's leading pull can be imitated by classical signals, and every strategy is limited to a rate falling at least as the inverse fourth power. Exact, continuous error correction shields the masses from noise but hides them from each other: the best rate falls as the inverse seventh power, and six positions on a hexagon come within 10% of it at large separation.

item.title: Entanglement distillation, nonlocal magic, and state sharing in an isospectral non-Hermitian bipartite model
item.description:
Chenhuan Wu

An invertible nonunitary similarity deformation leaves a two-qubit Hamiltonian's spectrum unchanged while varying a selected normalized right eigenstate in the fixed physical inner product. We embed this state in a two-parameter maximally correlated family that includes local dephasing and noisy circuit preparation. Hashing and a matching diagonal relative-entropy bound give the exact distillable entanglement and the PPT comparison distances at every finite tensor power. Correlated PPT catalysts cannot improve the Bell-pair distillation rate. The optimized CHSH value is \(2\sqrt{1+t^2}\): every state with nonzero coherence violates CHSH, while complete dephasing is separable. A calibrated finite-sample bound and two equal-fidelity preparations clarify which noise parameters determine the rate. For pure inputs, the binomial Schmidt spectrum gives logarithmic collectively optimized nonlocal magic with vanishing density, despite a positive entanglement density and extensive pairwise-frame magic. Fixed Clifford decoding gives six- and eight-copy CCZ concentration probabilities \(P_6=\frac12(1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ})\) and \(P_8=1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ}\). The same family permits explicit swapping recursions, symmetry-resolved entanglement, and a comparison of qubit stabilizer and fermionic Gaussian resources. These calculations keep the relevant operation classes separate when comparing many-copy limits.

item.title: Vanishing Relative Distance of Uniformly Random CSS LDPC Codes Built from Permutation Matrices
item.description:
Kenta Kasai

Classical random regular low-density parity-check codes can have minimum distance growing linearly with block length. We study CSS check matrices formed as full $J\times L$ arrays of arbitrary $P\times P$ permutation matrices, sampled uniformly subject to commutation. For fixed column weight $J\ge3$ and fixed even row weight $L>2J$, we prove that the relative minimum distance converges to zero in probability as $P\to\infty$, with block length $n=LP$. We analyze the weight enumerators that count all nontrivial logical representatives after excluding stabilizers. A coefficientwise lower bound shows that, at every fixed relative weight $0<α<1$ along even-weight sequences, exponentially many such representatives exist with high probability. Their typical and mean counts have exponent lower bound $h_2(α)/2$, where $h_2$ is the binary entropy function. We compare this bound with the classical LDPC and dense CSS mean weight-distribution exponents. The existence, with high probability, of a logical operator below every fixed target weight $δn$ yields the distance conclusion.

item.title: TCBP-JOBS: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Error Correction Decoding and Noise Learning with Near-Optimal Accuracy
item.description:
Ben Howe, Satvik Maurya, Jan Olle, Ivan Basov, Muyuan Li, Justin G. Lietz, und 2 weitere

Achieving near-optimal quantum error correction (QEC) decoding accuracy often requires computationally expensive searches that limit both large-scale simulation and real-time operation. We introduce trajectory-calibrated belief propagation (TCBP), which learns calibrated fault probabilities from BP trajectories, and jittered OSD beam search (JOBS), which uses these probabilities to guide parallel GPU searches. Across surface, color and bivariate-bicycle code memory and surgery circuits, TCBP-JOBS achieves logical error rates comparable to those of the Tesseract most-likely-error decoder at physical error rates of 0.1% to 0.4%, and up to 4.5$\times$ lower on the largest codes. Serial speedups over Tesseract's sparsified presets range from 10$\times$ to 7,400$\times$, and against unsparsified long-beam Tesseract they reach 13,000$\times$ on the bivariate-bicycle codes, at logical error rate ratios of 0.97 to 1.57. At lower physical error rates ($10^{-4}$ to $5\times10^{-4}$), rare-event splitting on the gross code shows that Tesseract is more accurate. Batched execution accelerates offline simulation for rapid, efficient exploration of large-scale QEC design spaces. For QPUs with longer logical clock cycles, our serial memory and logical-surgery experiments demonstrate accuracy comparable to Tesseract while meeting the millisecond-scale latency requirements of online feed-forward operation. Beyond memory and logic decoding, we demonstrate using TCBP-JOBS for confidence scores for postselection in memory and magic-state cultivation, enabling end-to-end color code cultivation. Together, these methods provide a GPU framework for accelerating QEC research via accurate decoding, noise estimation, and confidence assessment.

item.title: Specifying & Verifying Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
item.description:
Stavan Jain, Nithin Raveendran, Aws Albarghouthi

Building quantum computers is challenging due to the noise that affects qubits. Quantum error correction tackles noise by encoding information in quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes. These codes are often complex, increasingly found by computational search, presented in diverse formalisms with informal arguments, and hard to reason about algorithmically. Given that the rest of the quantum computing stack relies on a QEC code's properties for correct computation, we propose a formally verified foundation for QEC codes. We present QECLean, a Lean-based framework for formally specifying and verifying QEC codes. QECLean backs every claimed QEC-code property with a machine-checked proof, unifies the diverse presentations of codes in the literature through common abstractions, and makes new codes easy to specify. We present a new compositional technique, code combinators, for proving code distance analytically. Code combinators allow us to prove the distance of large codes that are out of reach for algorithmic techniques; for example, we show that IBM's $[[360, 12, \leq 24]]$ code has distance 24, which was previously only known as an upper bound. Furthermore, we show how our approach allows us to formalize and prove entire code families, such as the surface code. Our work lays the foundation required for reasoning about circuit-level implementations of codes on given architectures and for building end-to-end verified compilers for quantum computers. QECLean is available at https://github.com/Stavan-Jain/QECLean

item.title: Stabilizer-Restricted Antidistinguishability in Quantum Computation with Magic States
item.description:
Selman Ipek

An antidistinguishing measurement for a family of preparations excludes at least one preparation for every possible outcome, constraining 'classical' representations of these processes, known as ontological models. We develop this connection within quantum computing with magic states (QCM), a universal model of quantum computation. Our constructions use adaptive Pauli measurements on tensor products of single-qubit non stabilizer states, including families associated with the Clifford hierarchy. These constructions yield stabilizer-restricted versions of the Pusey-Barrett-Rudolph theorem: any ontological model reproducing these measurement statistics and satisfying preparation independence must assign disjoint ontic supports to the preparations considered. We demonstrate this obstruction to preparation independence in a concrete ontological model based on convex polytopes used for the classical simulation of QCM.

item.title: Closing the loop on memory: accurate, shallow and transferable decoding of quantum LDPC codes
item.description:
Zhou You, Ying Li, Xiao Yuan, Yuan Yao

Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have attracted interest for fault-tolerant quantum computing because their high-rate constructions offer a route to reduced qubit overhead. Realizing this potential requires reliable decoding. Belief propagation (BP) forms the basis of many qLDPC decoders, but can fail to converge under circuit-level noise. Memory-based variants can improve convergence, yet selecting memory strengths that work reliably across different syndromes remains challenging. Here we introduce TEMPO-BP, which adapts each variable's memory strength to the evolving decoding state through local feedback. On the gross code at a physical error rate of 0.4%, single-run TEMPO-BP achieves a per-shot logical failure rate of 0.73%, compared with 2.51% for BP+OSD+CS-10. Ensembles of 10-15 concurrent instances match or lower failure counts relative to Relay-BP-5 at all ten tested operating points, with per-instance iteration caps at least tenfold lower than its serial limit. Without retuning, the gross-code parameters yield fewer observed failures than Relay-BP-5 in its published gross-code configuration across four additional code families. Ablations support state-dependent memory control, while a loop-gain analysis characterizes specific amplification modes in the decoding dynamics.

item.title: Metrological Channels Induced by Encrypted Quantum Cloning: Optimal-Probe Fisher-Information Broadcasting and Single-Use Operational Recovery
item.description:
Nalan Kandirmaz

Encrypted quantum cloning creates multiple individually inaccessible signal systems from which an unknown input state can be recovered by combining any selected signal with a shared quantum key. Here we study parameter estimation when a local sensing transformation is applied after encrypted cloning and before decryption. For the two-clone qubit protocol, a local Pauli rotation on one encrypted signal is shown to induce, after standard decryption, a parameter-dependent Pauli dephasing channel rather than a unitary rotation. We derive its Pauli-transfer representation and the corresponding quantum Fisher information (QFI) for arbitrary mixed qubit probes. We then distinguish raw QFI, which for an optimal decoded probe may remain simultaneously present in a decoded output and its complement, from decoder-accessible QFI, which is operationally single-use because a first decryption destroys the shared syndrome information needed for a second standard recovery. For $n\geq2$ encrypted clones, the effective channel family is independent of clone number up to a clone-parity-dependent permutation of the Pauli axes (the single-clone case is exceptional for $Y$-sensing, where the decoded map stays unitary). This produces a metrological parity switch: for fixed probe and generator, even and odd clone numbers can yield respectively vanishing and maximal QFI. Closed expressions are obtained for the degradation of this parity contrast under probe depolarization and Pauli-diagonal Bloch-vector contraction.

item.title: Relaxation Critical Dynamics of Strong-to-Weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking
item.description:
Jiaqiang Li, Xianquan Yan, Han-Ze Li, Shuai Yin, Shuo Liu

Strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB) is unique to mixed states: strong symmetry is broken while weak symmetry is preserved, requiring two order parameters.
